_note: What `inject::safe_name` makes of a file's name, as one shared fixture
for two test suites - the same device as requests.json, applied to a
pure function instead of to a vocabulary.
The Kotlin half (HandoffTest) asserts `Handoff.Files.preview` produces
these. The Rust half (apexd/apex-agent-core/tests/android_safe_names.rs)
asserts `inject::safe_name` produces them. Neither half alone is worth
anything: a Kotlin mirror of a Rust function, checked by a Kotlin author,
agrees with whatever that author believed - which is exactly how this app
was twice wrong about the protocol.
null means the daemon REFUSES the name rather than repairing it, and the
phone shows Handoff.Files.UNUSABLE_NAME. A preview that answered `file..`
for `..` would promise a file the user is never going to find.
The four control-byte keys carry a real control byte each (LF, BEL, TAB,
DEL). They are refused rather than reduced, for the reason
NameError::ControlByte gives: a user who typed one into a filename has
either made a mistake worth seeing, or is being used by something that
made the name for them.
Writing this found three divergences in a first draft that looked
obviously right: `..` was repaired instead of refused; e-acute was
guessed as two underscores and is one; and an emoji really is TWO
replacements in a Kotlin loop over Char and ONE in a Rust loop over
chars(), which is why preview() walks code points.
